title: What Zelensky must learn from war leaders past
gist: By 11 June 2026 the Ukraine war had run 1,569 days — longer than the First World War or the Soviet Great Patriotic War — and Zelensky's July purge of Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov (35, drone-first) followed six days later by armed forces chief Oleksandr Syrskyi (60, Soviet-trained) reads as strength, not weakness, on the Lincoln/Churchill precedent of serial command sackings. The decisive military variable is not drones per se but their integration into a digital network of FPV craft, cyber, EW jamming and real-time human and drone intelligence.

insights.claim: On 11 June 2026 the Ukraine conflict was recorded at 1,569 days — longer than the First World War, the 1861-65 American Civil War and the Soviet Union's 1941-45 Great Patriotic War, equivalent for British forces of 1939 to reaching late 1943.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: If the WWII analogy holds, the war is nearer its decisive phase than its start — a duration anchor for anyone pricing Ukraine reconstruction, defence procurement or ceasefire odds.

insights.claim: The popular First World War analogies — attrition, trenches, heavy artillery, or the arrival of wonder weapons — miss the real value of comparison, which is the learning curve rather than the hardware.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: Judge defence-tech winners by integration and adaptation speed, not by which novel platform gets headlines.

insights.claim: All long conflicts produce a steep learning curve in which commanders test which combinations of equipment work; even on the first day of the Somme different tactics produced successes in the south and night attacks began within days.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: Expect continual doctrine churn in Ukraine; procurement bets on any single fixed tactical concept decay fast.

insights.so_what: Faster adaptation is not translating into cheaper war in blood — sustaining manpower, not technology, is the binding constraint.

insights.claim: John Keegan's The Face of Battle (1976) argued that soldiers at Agincourt, Waterloo and the Somme carried identical hopes, fears and jealousies despite radically different equipment — the constant across military revolutions is the human being.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: A reusable filter for hype: technology changes the tools, not the human system that must absorb them.

insights.claim: Historically, new weapons only paid off when integrated: British tanks failed at Flers-Courcelette in 1916 and Cambrai in 1917 despite achieving surprise, and only won at Amiens in 1918 when combined with infantry, artillery and aircraft.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: Systems integrators, not point-solution hardware vendors, capture the value in a military-technology cycle.

insights.claim: The Battle of Britain equivalent was Hugh Dowding's network — Spitfires and Hurricanes fused with radar, human observers, anti-aircraft guns and fighter controllers in headquarters.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: Command-and-control networks are the historical template for today's battlefield software layer — the durable moat above the airframe.

insights.so_what: The investable layer is EW, comms and battlefield data fusion — not just airframes and munitions.

insights.claim: Drones alone cannot win the war because terrain still has to be taken and held by people, echoing TR Fehrenbach's dictum that defending land requires putting young men into the mud.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: Manpower and ground-holding capability remain the scarce input; drone-only theories of victory are incomplete.

insights.claim: Logistics were as decisive as front-line fighting in the Western Desert of 1942-43 and North-West Europe in 1944-45, and British ports and railways only realised their full potential in 1916 when railway manager Eric Geddes was made Director General of Military Railways.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: Civilian logistics expertise inserted into military command is a historically proven force multiplier — a template for wartime industrial mobilisation.

insights.claim: On 15 July Zelensky sacked popular Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, triggering street protests, resignations by military officers and officials, and placards reading 'Hands off Fedorov' and 'Stop sabotaging victory!'
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: Ukrainian domestic political risk now moves on defence-personnel decisions, a variable for aid-flow and reform-conditionality watchers.
insights.locator: In response, several military officers and officials resigned

insights.claim: The split was generational and doctrinal: Fedorov, 35, championed drones and high-tech warfare while Syrskyi, 60, represented the Soviet-trained generation believing in low-tech tanks, aircraft and personnel, a strategy that produced catastrophic Ukrainian casualties.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: The winner of this doctrinal fight sets Ukraine's procurement mix between legacy heavy platforms and unmanned systems.
insights.locator: Fedorov’s political end was caused by tensions

insights.claim: After renewed street protests Zelensky reversed course and sacked Syrskyi too on 21 July, with a Kyiv opinion poll showing 55 per cent of Ukrainians agreed with the dismissal.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: Public opinion is still a binding constraint on Ukrainian wartime executive power — a signal that democratic conditionality for Western aid remains credible.
insights.locator: The president reconsidered, and Syrskyi also found himself sacked

insights.claim: Neither commander solved Ukraine's manpower crisis, with an alleged two million people in hiding or abroad escaping conscription and an estimated 200,000 service personnel gone AWOL.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: Manpower depletion at this scale caps any offensive theory of victory and strengthens the case for capital-for-labour substitution via automation.
insights.locator: Frankly, Zelensky needs both men

insights.claim: Fedorov, previously Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Digital Transformation before becoming Defence Minister in January, persuaded Elon Musk to stop Russia using Starlink satellites for drone attacks, causing considerable disruption to Russian frontline and drone operations.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: Commercial satcom access is an active lever in the war — SpaceX policy decisions have direct battlefield consequences.

themes.theme: Ruthless command churn as a winning trait

insights.claim: Military historian Richard Holmes' answer to how to be a top general at the end of a war — 'don't be one at the beginning' — captures the rule that long conflicts inevitably fire their commanders mid-term.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: Treat leadership turnover in a long war as a base-rate event, not as evidence of institutional collapse.
insights.locator: When asked how to be a top general

insights.claim: Lincoln sacked or accepted resignations from Winfield Scott, Irvin McDowell, George McClellan, Ambrose Burnside and Joseph Hooker before finding a winning combination in Meade, Sherman and Grant — ruthlessness that underlined rather than undermined his leadership.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: The historical base rate says command churn precedes victory, so Zelensky's purge is a weak signal for Russian advantage.
insights.locator: To win the Civil War for the Union side

insights.claim: The pattern repeated in both world wars: Britain's CIGS changed four times between 1914-18, Churchill sacked Ironside and Dill before settling with Alan Brooke in December 1941, and Dowding was forced out of Fighter Command in November 1940 despite having just won the Battle of Britain.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: Even successful commanders get purged in wartime politics — personnel news is a poor proxy for battlefield trajectory.

insights.claim: The British Eighth Army burned through four Western Desert commanders in under two years before Montgomery took over on 15 August 1942, restored calm, resisted Churchill's whims and beat the Germans.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: Multiple failed appointments before the right one is the norm; patience with turnover, not stability for its own sake, is what correlates with winning.
insights.locator: These crises of command also spread to the campaign

insights.claim: Zelensky's command changes signal strength rather than weakness because he is following the Lincoln pattern while also responding to democratic pressure from the streets — a contrast with Russia, where similar protests would bring arrests and detention.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: Directly contradicts the market narrative that Kyiv's political turbulence benefits Moscow.
insights.quote: President Zelensky’s changes do not smack of weakness, but of strength.

insights.claim: Putin's KGB background and prior command over Russian deployments in Chechnya, Syria and Crimea makes him the Jefferson Davis of this conflict, while Zelensky's lack of formal army education or administrative experience makes him the Lincoln.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: A named historical analogue that implies the militarily credentialed leader is not the favourite.
